opening.headline: To prevent previously working scenarios from breaking after switching models, it's necessary to understand how failures encountered during operations should be incorporated into the evaluation set.
body: As agents are improved, overall success rates remain similar, but some scenarios that previously worked suddenly start failing. Such regressions are often first reported by users, and only then does the team begin the process of reproduction and investigation.

This course compares offline evaluation using a predefined dataset before deployment with online evaluation that scores actual records from an operating agent. It also examines step-by-step the process of creating a regression evaluation set that captures failures encountered once and prevents their recurrence.

As of 2026-10: The OpenAI Evals·grader example in this lesson is an example of reading a deprecated interface. The existing Evals will be read-only from October 31st and will be retired on November 30th, so configure the new evaluation pipeline with other execution tools and transfer evaluation data and criteria.

The process of creating an evaluation set from operational data can be divided into steps.

visual.alt: The overall success rate before and after model replacement is similar, but in two specific scenarios, the outcomes changed from success to failure.

paragraphs: After updating the agent's model to a new version, the overall success rate remained similar to before. However, several days later, user complaints began to emerge, reporting that certain scenarios that previously worked are no longer functioning.

The team should now begin by reproducing the issue. They must trace whether the failure occurs under a specific input, due to a change, or because the system was originally unstable. Without evaluation, the team has no way to verify whether a change has broken something else, and ends up working in a reactive manner—waiting for the issue to occur, manually reproducing it, fixing it, and hoping nothing else is broken. The ADK document also recommends automating agent evaluation due to these limitations.
What is needed is a mechanism to prevent a fixed failure from reoccurring. This is the question this lesson addresses. How can failures encountered in operations be mitigated in evaluation?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: The overall average is similar, but if only some scenarios failed, could we have detected this regression based solely on average metrics? I'll revisit this answer when the class ends.

screens.outro: First, let me recall where failures are going in my operating environment.

screens.title: Where do failures encountered during operation go?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't enter or submit your answer, so think for yourself first and then click.

items.prompt: Where are the failure cases discovered during operations currently being recorded?
items.answer: If a failure is recorded only in the issue tracker or conversation logs, no one will remember the example during the next change. A failure must be preserved in a form that can be re-executed later—specifically, as a task with defined inputs and expected outputs—so it can be evaluated.

items.prompt: Is this example executed again before the next deployment?
items.answer: If it doesn't fail again, the same failure could return at any time. Evaluation should not be a one-time check after reporting but rather automatically re-run every time there's a change. Manual verification is the first thing to be eliminated during busy deployments.

items.prompt: Have you ever encountered the same failure twice?
items.answer: If the same failure occurs twice, it means the first failure was not reflected in the evaluation. The core principle of this course is that any incorrect attempt is included in the evaluation set, and thus identical failures are filtered out thereafter before deployment.

screens.outro: After organizing my thoughts, I'll first compare two types of evaluations—those before and after deployment.

screens.title: Offline and online evaluations
screens.lead: Compare offline evaluation and online evaluation by examining when each takes place and what they target.

states.label: offline evaluation
states.body: An evaluation that compares results before deployment using a predefined dataset. Each time the prompt or tool configuration changes, the same input is rerun to compare before-and-after outcomes. ADK keeps evaluation cases in files and enables local, repeated execution, making it akin to unit testing in agent development. Google Cloud also evaluates agents during local development iterations and guides deployed agents to be checked against recorded traces or synthetic benchmarks. The advantage is that controlled inputs make result comparisons easy and fast to repeat, while the limitation is that it cannot observe new inputs not present in the dataset. Thus, offline evaluation serves as the first checkpoint to verify whether changes are safe before deployment.

states.label: online assessment
states.body: An evaluation that asynchronously scores the actual traces of running agents. Google Cloud's online monitor periodically checks, typically every 10 minutes, sampling traces and logs that match certain conditions, computing metrics and recording the results in logs and monitoring systems. It adjusts costs by setting sample ratios and the maximum number of items evaluated at once. This is well-suited for detecting quality drift—gradual degradation due to user behavior or external data changes. To enable this, agents must export signals such as inputs, outputs, and tool definitions via OpenTelemetry. Because online evaluation uses real user inputs, it provides a pathway for discovering new failures missed by offline evaluations.

screens.outro: The two evaluations do not replace each other. Next, we will examine the regression evaluation set designed to maintain backward compatibility.

screens.title: What is a regression evaluation set?
screens.lead: The table below compares capability assessment and regression assessment. Read each row to verify how the roles of the two assessments differ.

data.caption: Comparison of capability assessment and regression assessment
rows: A task for an agent to fully process a complex request it has yet to master
A task to reprocess a previously fixed failure case, alongside typical requests that were already being handled well
What does this agent do well?
Does the system still process tasks as it did previously?
The starting point of pass rate
Start low. Provide a target that gradually increases in difficulty, targeting tasks that are challenging for the agent.
This means there is still room for improvement.
Since there is a signal that something has broken, the cause must be identified immediately.
Higher pass rates result in graduation via regression evaluation.
When reaching 100%, saturation results in backward movement being monitored but no improvement signals being provided.
data.notes: The last row of the table is important. Evaluation does not end once a capability is established—it evolves based on the agent's maturity. During improvement, capability evaluation provides direction; after improvement is complete, the same task transitions into regression evaluation to maintain performance. Once the agent is released and refined, a high-passing capability evaluation graduates into regression evaluation. What initially asked "Can it do this?" eventually shifts to "Can it still do this stably?" Throughout the process of improving performance, regression evaluation must also be run concurrently to ensure that no other components break.

screens.outro: Since we've verified the role of the regression evaluation set, let's now examine the process by which operational failures enter into it.

screens.title: Flow of operational failure entering regression set
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to verify the five steps from failure encountered in operation until it becomes one item in the evaluation set.

visual.alt: A cyclic flow where a failure is selected from operation logs, converted into a task, added to the evaluation set, and then re-executed after each change.
labels: Collection of operational logs and trace data
Execute evaluation set after each change

steps.title: 1. Collection of operational logs and trace data
steps.body: During development, you must record everything in order to later extract good evaluation examples. Without records, you cannot reconstruct what inputs and tool calls were made when encountering a failure. Recording inputs, outputs, and tool calls as traces is the starting point.

steps.title: 2. Prioritization of significant failures
steps.body: Start with failures that have significant impact among user reports and support inquiries. Attempting to evaluate all failures at once would never conclude. Begin with failures that occur frequently or cause substantial damage, then gradually expand from there.

steps.title: 3. Convert task to expected outcome
steps.body: Replace ambiguous failure traces with clear tasks and expected outcomes. A good task is one that two experts independently arrive at the same pass/fail determination. Alongside, include a reference solution that demonstrates a valid approach.

steps.title: 4. Start small
steps.body: You don't need hundreds from the start. Twenty to fifty simple tasks drawn from actual failures are a good starting point. During early development, changes have a significant impact, so differences can be observed even with a small sample size. However, evaluation becomes more difficult the later it is introduced.

steps.title: 5. Restart and Continuous Execution
steps.body: After making changes, re-run the evaluation set to verify whether the task passes or if the original task remains unchanged. Then, execute the evaluation set alongside all changes. OpenAI introduces this process as a cycle of evaluation-driven continuous improvement, explaining that evaluation results lead to the next round of improvements. This cycle must continue for the evaluation set to gradually approach real-world operational conditions.

screens.outro: Now that we understand the flow, let's proceed by applying it according to actual examples.

screens.title: Analysis: New failure type discovered, evaluation set added, reevaluation performed
screens.lead: The instructor explains a hypothetical case step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: After replacing the model, the agent generates incorrect tool arguments in requests with a date format different from the usual. Since the existing offline evaluation dataset does not contain such requests, there were no warnings before deployment.

steps.title: Step 1: Discovery
steps.body: A low rating from online monitoring and a user report point to the same trace. Since both signals point to the same location, it can be concluded that this is not a coincidence but a new failure type. Online evaluation identifies the inputs that were missed by the offline evaluation set.

steps.title: Step 2: Add to evaluation set
steps.body: Input this trace as a clear task with well-defined input and expected tool arguments, and include it in the regression evaluation set. Adding a few more date formats similar to this will also allow capturing variations of the same type. Failure at this stage becomes part of the evaluation.

steps.title: Step 3: Reevaluation
steps.body: After modifying agent or tool descriptions, re-evaluate the evaluation set offline. Verify whether the newly added tasks pass, and whether existing tasks continue to pass. Issues where changes in one area cause failures in another are filtered out at this stage.

steps.title: Step 4: Continuation
steps.body: In all subsequent changes, this task will be executed together. If the same failure reoccurs, it will be detected before deployment, eliminating the need to wait for user reports. A cycle of failure detection has now been established within the evaluation set. In this example, only one new task has been added; however, by incrementally adding failures in the same manner, the evaluation set will gradually resemble operational reality.

screens.outro: Finally, we will examine methods for creating a balanced evaluation set.

screens.title: Explanation: Creating a Balanced Regression Set
screens.lead: When an item is selected, the instructor's explanation is displayed. Check one by one the common points often overlooked when opening the evaluation set.

items.prompt: Is collecting only operational failures sufficient?
items.answer: Focusing only on operational failures will only accumulate failure paths in the evaluation set and exclude successful paths. By including representative examples of normal operation, you can determine whether changes have inadvertently broken previously working components.

items.prompt: What happens if only one case is captured?
items.answer: An evaluation that considers only one scenario optimizes only for that single case. For example, an agent that checks only when a search is needed could be created for nearly every query. In Anthropic's web search case, they balanced the evaluation by including both queries that require searching and those that require answering based on existing knowledge.

items.prompt: How should the evaluation environment be managed?
items.answer: Each attempt must begin with a clean environment. If there are shared states such as leftover files or caches between attempts, failures that should be independent will occur simultaneously due to the same root cause, leading instead to environment-related issues rather than agent performance issues.

items.prompt: What happens when the evaluation set reaches 100%?
items.answer: When evaluations approach 100%, regression occurs despite supervision, and no improvement signals are provided. This state is referred to as evaluation saturation. While maintaining regression-based evaluations, new, more challenging tasks must be introduced to reestablish improvement goals. Anthropic explains that when evaluations get close to 100%, even significant capability improvements may appear only as minor differences, potentially leading to misinterpretation of results.

screens.outro: I will conclude by summarizing the contents so far.

screens.title: A single mistake is included in the evaluation set.
screens.lead: Let's revisit the initial question by reflecting on the flow of the lesson.

paragraphs: Offline evaluation uses a dataset predefined before deployment, while online evaluation assesses quality using actual operational records. The two evaluations are separated to cover pre-deployment and post-deployment periods.

The regression test suite preserves previous behaviors and converts failures encountered during operations into clear, unambiguous tasks that are then incorporated into the suite. Once a test fails, the test suite remembers not to fail again. The initial question—whether regression could be detected solely based on average metrics—is no. To reveal regressions in certain scenarios, the test suite must contain the scenarios that are intended to be preserved.

glossary.def: An evaluation that runs the agent with the predefined dataset before deployment to compare the state before and after changes.
An evaluation that continuously monitors quality changes by assessing the actual records of running agents.
A set of evaluations to verify that tasks previously being processed are still being processed. The pass rate must be nearly 100%.
This is a phenomenon where the agent's quality gradually degrades due to changes in user behavior or external data.
The pass rate has reached 100%, and regression is being monitored, but no further improvement signals are being issued.

misconceptions.myth: Passing an offline evaluation means it is safe within operations.
misconceptions.fact: Offline evaluation sees only the inputs present in the dataset. New inputs from operations and time-related changes must be monitored online.

misconceptions.myth: Once you create the evaluation set, you are done.
misconceptions.fact: Whenever a new failure is encountered during operation, it should be added to the evaluation set and trained on. The evaluation set is a continuously growing asset.

misconceptions.myth: An evaluation set must consist of hundreds before it can begin.
misconceptions.fact: Starting with a simple task set of 20 to 50 tasks derived from actual failures yields significant benefits. The evaluation becomes more difficult the later the tasks are created.

closing.lead: This summarizes the core content covered in this course.
points: Offline evaluation occurs before deployment, while online evaluation checks agents during operations.
The regression evaluation set maintains nearly 100% pass rate and indicates regression.
Failures discovered during operation are converted into clear tasks and added to the evaluation set.
Once a mistake is made, it is re-executed every time subsequent changes are applied to the evaluation set.
closing.reflectionLead: Finally, here's a question for you to think about on your own. Please feel free to recall it at your convenience—no submission or grading is required.
closing.reflection: Among the failures encountered in recent operations, what is not currently included in the evaluation set, and what form of task could it be converted into?

title: Online and offline evaluation and regression datasets

checks.q: The pass rate of the regression evaluation set dropped noticeably on a certain day. What does this signal mean?
options: There is plenty of room for improvement, meaning it should now be evaluated through capability assessment.
It suggests a high likelihood that something previously being handled has broken.
This means the evaluation is saturated and has no further meaning.
This means turning off online evaluation and conducting evaluation only offline.
checks.explain: A regression test suite is intended to ensure that previously working tasks continue to function, and thus its pass rate should be nearly 100%. A drop indicates that something has been disrupted or changed.

wrong.0: Capability assessment starts with a low pass rate and serves as an improvement goal, which is different in meaning from the decline observed in regression assessment.
wrong.2: Saturation has reached 100% throughput and is no longer providing any improvement signals. This is opposite to a decline.
wrong.3: The two evaluations do not handle a replacement relationship; instead, they are assigned separately to before and after deployment.

checks.explain: There must be records to trace failures, and failures must be clearly defined as distinct tasks before they can be included in an evaluation set; after fixes and re-execution, each subsequent change must be re-run to detect recurrence.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The order is incorrect. Remember that you must first have records to identify failures, and then you must clearly define those failures as distinct tasks before including them in the evaluation set.
